TRADEMARK FAIR USE — NOMINATIVE AND CLASSIC (DESCRIPTIVE) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Ridgeline Auto Service, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS TRADEMARK FAIR USE INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes the two trademark fair use doctrines that federal courts sitting in California apply when a person uses someone else's trademark: the statutory "classic" or descriptive fair use defense codified at 15 U.S.C. section 1115(b)(4), which applies when a defendant uses a term that is also another's mark to describe the defendant's own goods or services; and the judicially created "nominative" fair use doctrine of New Kids on the Block v. News America Publishing, Inc., which applies when a defendant uses another's mark to refer to the trademark holder's own product, person, or event. It sets out the statutory text of the classic defense; the Supreme Court's holding in KP Permanent Make-Up, Inc. v. Lasting Impression I, Inc. that a fair use defendant carries no burden to negate likelihood of confusion and that some consumer confusion is compatible with fair use; the three-factor nominative fair use test of New Kids; Cairns v. Franklin Mint Co.'s explanation of which analysis applies to which kind of use and of the relationship between each defense and the Ninth Circuit's AMF Inc. v. Sleekcraft Boats likelihood-of-confusion factors; Playboy Enterprises, Inc. v. Welles's application of the test to website headlines, banner advertisements, metatags, and a repeated watermark; Toyota Motor Sales, U.S.A., Inc. v. Tabari's application of the doctrine to internet domain names, its allocation of the burden of proof after KP Permanent, and its limits on the scope of a trademark injunction; and the statutory fair use exclusions from federal and California trademark dilution law, 15 U.S.C. section 1125(c)(3) and Business and Professions Code section 14247. It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning Ridgeline Auto Service, Inc., with respect to the following mark owned by Acme Motor Company: The word mark "ACME" and associated logo, U.S. Reg. No. 1,234,567, and the following use of that mark: The phrase "independent ACME repair specialists" on shop signage and in website text. This Information Sheet describes what the cited statutes and decisions say; it does not itself determine whether any particular use is nominative, descriptive, fair, or infringing, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination.

THE STATUTORY ("CLASSIC") FAIR USE DEFENSE: 15 U.S.C. § 1115(B)(4)
Section 33 of the Lanham Act, 15 U.S.C. section 1115, governs the evidentiary effect of a federal trademark registration. Subsection (b) provides that where the right to use a registered mark has become incontestable under section 1065, the registration is conclusive evidence of the validity of the mark, of the registration, of the registrant's ownership, and of the registrant's exclusive right to use the mark in commerce, but that this conclusive evidence remains "subject to proof of infringement as defined in section 1114" and subject to nine listed defenses or defects. The fourth of those defenses, section 1115(b)(4), is the statutory fair use defense: it applies where the use charged to be an infringement is a use "otherwise than as a mark" of the party's own individual name in the party's own business, of the individual name of someone in privity with that party, or of a term or device that is descriptive of and used fairly and in good faith only to describe that party's goods or services or their geographic origin. The same list contains other defenses that are not fair use, including fraudulent procurement of the registration, abandonment, use of the mark to misrepresent source, prior continuous use in a limited area, prior registration, antitrust violation, functionality, and equitable principles including laches, estoppel, and acquiescence. Courts refer to the section 1115(b)(4) defense as the "classic" or descriptive fair use defense, and it is the defense that applies when a defendant uses a word that happens to be another's mark to describe the defendant's own product rather than the trademark holder's.

A FAIR USE DEFENDANT HAS NO BURDEN TO NEGATE LIKELIHOOD OF CONFUSION (KP PERMANENT MAKE-UP)
In KP Permanent Make-Up, Inc. v. Lasting Impression I, Inc., the United States Supreme Court resolved a split among the Courts of Appeals over whether a defendant raising the statutory fair use defense must show that its use is unlikely to confuse consumers. Both parties sold permanent makeup and both used some version of the term "micro color"; the registrant's "Micro Colors" registration had become incontestable. The Ninth Circuit had held that no use could be recognized as fair where consumer confusion was probable and appeared to place on the fair use defendant the burden of showing the absence of confusion. The Supreme Court vacated that judgment. It reasoned from two textual fixed points: section 1115(b) places the burden of proving likelihood of confusion on the party charging infringement even when that party relies on an incontestable registration, and Congress said nothing about likelihood of confusion in setting out the elements of the fair use defense in section 1115(b)(4). The Court added that it would make no sense to give a defendant an affirmative defense consisting of showing that the plaintiff cannot prove an element of its own case, because a defendant that merely leaves the factfinder unpersuaded is already entitled to judgment on that element.

SOME CONSUMER CONFUSION IS COMPATIBLE WITH FAIR USE, AND ITS EXTENT MAY STILL MATTER (KP PERMANENT MAKE-UP)
Having placed the burden of proving likelihood of confusion on the trademark owner, the Supreme Court in KP Permanent Make-Up drew the further conclusion that some possibility of consumer confusion must be compatible with fair use. The Court traced that tolerance to the common law and to the nature of descriptive marks: a descriptive term qualifies for registration only after it takes on secondary meaning, and the registrant then obtains an exclusive right not in the original descriptive sense of the words but only in the secondary sense associated with the registrant's goods. The Court described the Lanham Act as adopting a similar leniency, finding no indication that the statute was meant to deprive commercial speakers of the ordinary utility of descriptive words, and it quoted the Second Circuit for the proposition that a plaintiff who chooses to identify its product with a well-known descriptive phrase accepts the risk of resulting confusion. At the same time, the Court declined to hold that the degree of likely confusion is irrelevant: its holding that fair use can occur alongside some degree of confusion does not foreclose considering the extent of likely confusion in assessing whether a defendant's use is objectively fair, and the Court expressly reserved the question whether "used fairly" demands only that the descriptive term describe the goods accurately.

WHY NOMINATIVE USE LIES OUTSIDE TRADEMARK LAW'S STRICTURES (NEW KIDS ON THE BLOCK)
New Kids on the Block v. News America Publishing, Inc. arose from newspaper telephone polls asking readers which member of the band was the most popular; the band sued for trademark infringement and related claims. The Ninth Circuit began from the proposition that a trademark is a limited property right in a particular word, phrase, or symbol, and that the primary cost of recognizing such rights is the removal of words from the language. That concern underlies the genericness rule and the descriptive fair use defense of section 1115(b)(4), which the court described as forbidding a registrant to appropriate a descriptive term for its exclusive use and thereby prevent others from accurately describing a characteristic of their goods. The court then identified a further category: cases in which many goods and services are effectively identifiable only by their trademarks, so that there is no descriptive substitute. It gave the example that one might refer to "the two-time world champions" or "the professional basketball team from Chicago," but it is far simpler to refer to the Chicago Bulls, and it pointed to its own earlier decision permitting an independent repair shop to use the Volkswagen mark to describe the cars it repaired. The court concluded that such uses are best understood as non-trademark uses of a mark, to which the infringement laws simply do not apply.

THE THREE-FACTOR NOMINATIVE FAIR USE TEST AND ITS BOUNDARY WITH CLASSIC FAIR USE (NEW KIDS ON THE BLOCK)
New Kids announced the test that the Ninth Circuit still applies. Where a defendant uses a trademark to describe the plaintiff's product rather than the defendant's own, a commercial user is entitled to a nominative fair use defense on three conditions: the product or service must be one not readily identifiable without use of the trademark; only so much of the mark may be used as is reasonably necessary to identify the product or service; and the user must do nothing that would, in conjunction with the mark, suggest sponsorship or endorsement by the trademark holder. A footnote to the second condition gave the illustration that a soft drink competitor would be entitled to compare its product to Coca-Cola or Coke but would not be entitled to use Coca-Cola's distinctive lettering. The court was explicit that it was not disturbing the statutory defense: this was not the classic fair use case in which the defendant uses the plaintiff's mark to describe the defendant's own product, and where a defendant's use of a mark refers to something other than the plaintiff's product the traditional fair use inquiry continues to govern. Applying its new test, the court held that the newspapers met all three conditions and that the first seven causes of action failed.

A NOMINATIVE USE MAY BE COMMERCIAL AND MAY COMPETE WITH THE MARK HOLDER (NEW KIDS ON THE BLOCK)
The band in New Kids argued that even if the newspapers could nominatively use the mark in their announcements, the pay-per-call polls themselves were money-making enterprises separate from the newspapers' reporting business, and that a nominative fair use defense should not apply where the use competes directly with the trademark holder, who ran its own pay-per-call lines. The Ninth Circuit rejected the argument. It held that where the use does not imply sponsorship or endorsement, the fact that it is carried on for profit and in competition with the trademark holder's business is beside the point, and that the trademark laws do not give a mark holder the right to channel the public's enthusiasm, or spending, only into items it has licensed or authorized. On the second and third conditions, the court observed that the newspapers referred to the band only to the extent necessary to identify it as the subject of the polls, did not use the band's distinctive logo, and said nothing that expressly or by fair implication connoted endorsement or joint sponsorship; it noted that one announcement implied the contrary by asking whether the band might be a turn off.

WHICH ANALYSIS APPLIES: WHOSE PRODUCT THE MARK DESCRIBES (CAIRNS V. FRANKLIN MINT)
Cairns v. Franklin Mint Co. arose from a fund established after the death of Diana, Princess of Wales, which sued a manufacturer of commemorative plates, dolls, and jewelry for false endorsement under 15 U.S.C. section 1125(a) and related claims. The Ninth Circuit used the case to draw the line between the two fair use doctrines. Classic fair use is present when the defendant has used the plaintiff's mark to describe the defendant's own product; nominative fair use is present when the defendant has used the plaintiff's mark to describe the plaintiff's product, for example for purposes of comparison. The distinction matters for two reasons the court identified: the two doctrines are governed by different analyses, and they stand in different relationships to the multi-factor likelihood-of-confusion test of AMF Inc. v. Sleekcraft Boats, with the classic fair use analysis complementing the Sleekcraft analysis and the nominative fair use analysis replacing it. The court also explained that the nominative analysis governs even when the defendant's ultimate goal is to describe its own product, so long as the mark is used to describe the plaintiff's product; that was true of New Kids itself, of the Volkswagen repair shop, of a broadcaster's references to the Boston Marathon, and of an imitator's comparison of its perfume to Chanel No. 5.

THE ELEMENTS OF THE CLASSIC FAIR USE DEFENSE AS THE NINTH CIRCUIT STATED THEM (CAIRNS V. FRANKLIN MINT)
Cairns set out the elements of the classic fair use defense by quoting the McCarthy treatise's reading of section 1115(b): the defendant's use of the term is not as a trademark or service mark; the defendant uses the term fairly and in good faith; and the defendant uses it only to describe its goods or services. The court described the underlying common law principle in the same terms the treatise used, that a junior user is always entitled to use a descriptive term in good faith in its primary, descriptive sense other than as a trademark. The court then stated the Ninth Circuit rule as it stood in 2002: the classic fair use defense is not available if there is a likelihood of customer confusion as to the origin of the product, citing Transgo, Inc. v. Ajac Transmission Parts Corp. and Lindy Pen Co. v. Bic Pen Corp. Two years later, in KP Permanent Make-Up, Inc. v. Lasting Impression I, Inc., the Supreme Court vacated a Ninth Circuit judgment resting on that view of the statutory defense, holding that the fair use defendant bears no burden to negate confusion and that some degree of confusion is compatible with fair use while the extent of likely confusion may still bear on whether the use is objectively fair.

HOW MUCH OF A MARK IS "REASONABLY NECESSARY" VARIES WITH THE USE (CAIRNS V. FRANKLIN MINT)
Applying the three factors to the Franklin Mint products, the Ninth Circuit held that the Princess was not readily identifiable without use of her name and likeness: one might refer to the English princess who died in a car crash in 1997, but it is far simpler and more likely to be understood to refer to Princess Diana. On the second factor the court held that what is reasonably necessary to identify the plaintiff's product differs from case to case, and that more use of a mark is reasonably necessary where the description of the defendant's product depends on the description of the plaintiff's product; it contrasted a district court decision finding that a book publisher used more of the "Godzilla" mark than necessary by setting the title in the mark holder's distinctive lettering, and another finding repeated use of "Barbie" and "Ken" reasonably necessary for purposes of parody. On the third factor the court observed that none of the advertisements claimed sponsorship or endorsement by the fund, that none carried a disclaimer, and that the same catalogue described other celebrity products as "authorized" by a trademark holder, which suggested that the Diana-related products were not. The court affirmed summary judgment for the manufacturer on the false endorsement claim.

expectedJSON.body: Having placed the burden of proving likelihood of confusion on the trademark owner, the Supreme Court in KP Permanent Make-Up drew the further conclusion that some possibility of consumer confusion must be compatible with fair use. The Court traced that tolerance to the common law and to the nature of descriptive marks: a descriptive term qualifies for registration only after it takes on secondary meaning, and the registrant then obtains an exclusive right not in the original descriptive sense of the words but only in the secondary sense associated with the registrant's goods. The Court described the Lanham Act as adopting a similar leniency, finding no indication that the statute was meant to deprive commercial speakers of the ordinary utility of descriptive words, and it quoted the Second Circuit for the proposition that a plaintiff who chooses to identify its product with a well-known descriptive phrase accepts the risk of resulting confusion. At the same time, the Court declined to hold that the degree of likely confusion is irrelevant: its holding that fair use can occur alongside some degree of confusion does not foreclose considering the extent of likely confusion in assessing whether a defendant's use is objectively fair, and the Court expressly reserved the question whether "used fairly" demands only that the descriptive term describe the goods accurately.

The Ninth Circuit held that a trademark injunction, particularly one involving nominative fair use, can raise serious First Amendment concerns because it can interfere with truthful communication between buyers and sellers, and that an injunction must be tailored to eliminate only the specific harm alleged. The injunction before it was overbroad because it barred domain names that on their face dispel any confusion about sponsorship, and it would remain overbroad even if limited to domains that do not expressly disclaim sponsorship, because the doctrine permits truthful use without an express disavowal so long as confusion as to sponsorship or endorsement is unlikely. The court added that the proper remedy for infringing use of a mark on a site generally falls short of prohibiting use of the site's domain name altogether, and that forced relinquishment of a domain is an extraordinary remedy. It vacated the injunction and remanded, instructing that a trademark injunction should be tailored to prevent ongoing violations rather than to punish past conduct, and that speakers do not lose the right to engage in permissible speech because they may have infringed in the past.

expectedJSON.body: Trademark dilution law contains its own express fair use exclusions, and they name nominative and descriptive fair use directly. The federal dilution statute, 15 U.S.C. section 1125(c)(3), provides that certain uses are not actionable as dilution by blurring or by tarnishment: any fair use, including a nominative or descriptive fair use or facilitation of such fair use, of a famous mark by another person other than as a designation of source for that person's own goods or services, including use in advertising or promotion that permits consumers to compare goods or services, and use identifying and parodying, criticizing, or commenting upon the famous mark owner or its goods or services; all forms of news reporting and news commentary; and any noncommercial use of a mark. California's Model State Trademark Law contains a parallel provision. Business and Professions Code section 14247, added by Statutes 2007, chapter 711, entitles the owner of a famous and distinctive mark to an injunction against another's commercial use that is likely to cause dilution, but excludes from liability the same three categories in nearly identical words, including any fair use, whether nominative or descriptive, other than as a designation of source for the user's own goods or services.
